author: Ian Young
title: "Big Brother monitoring everybody:" Flock camera debate heats up amid federal bill sponsorship - NewsBreak
text:
By Ian Young Ann Powell ,
1 hours ago
EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WEHT) — A Kentucky congressman plans to sponsor a bill to block funding for cities who use Flock cameras.
U.S. Representative Thomas Massie made the announcement on his X account this week. If passed, he says the bill will withhold federal money to departments that use Flock cameras.
“I’ve got one probably 60 yards away from my house,” says resident Chad Hoffman. “I know it is there and it is the right to privacy. It can absolutely be used for other things.”
1-year-old safely recovered after Owensboro vehicle theft Hoffman lives in Evansville and says the use of Flock cameras is going too far. While he understands law enforcement uses them to investigate and solve crimes he believes the cameras could be used for other things.
“I think that closed circuit television and CCTV, I think that it is just a Big Brother monitoring everybody,” says Hoffman.
However, law enforcement disagrees. Eyewitness News recently spoke with Vanderburgh County Sheriff Noah Robinson who says despite popular belief, Flock cameras are not used for mass surveillance.
Flock camera debate makes its way to Evansville “Our current technology does not allow for video capture,” says Robinson. “It does not allow for the capture of signals from cell phones. It does not allow for facial recognition, does not allow for person identification.”
According to Eyes Off Indiana, there are over 100 of these Flock cameras around Vanderburgh County. Around 70 of them are located within Evansville city limits.
Flock cameras continue to cause a national social media storm, and in some cases, people take matters into their own hands. In Texas authorities are searching for the person who hit a Flock camera and fled the scene.
Stolen property recovered, suspects arrested in Henderson In California sheriff deputies arrested a man they say vandalized several flock cameras. Here in southern Indiana, Indiana State Police say a flock camera was intentionally removed from I-69 just north of Evansville, but no one has been arrested.
Now a U.S. Congressman from Kentucky is weighing in. Representative Thomas Massie says he plans to sponsor a bill that would withhold federal money from municipalities and police departments that use flock cameras to surveil law‑abiding citizens.
While he is against the use of Flock cameras, Hoffman believes this approach is not the answer.
ISP says downed Flock camera was intentionally removed “I would not go that far.,” says Hoffman. “I do not think that defunding somebody is the right approach to get something to go away. I think that there are other measures that you can take.”
